result:
If I get one thing, I'd want to close the gap between what people actually want and what our collective machinery produces.

What strikes me most reading about human affairs isn't malice. It's how much of the world's suffering nobody chose. Wars that neither population wanted. Arms races where every participant would prefer to stop. Cities built for cars that no one enjoys sitting in traffic in. Industries almost everyone would be uncomfortable looking at directly, sustained by everyone's individual reasonable purchase. Nobody wakes up wanting these things, and yet here they are, stable, reproducing themselves year after year.

There's something almost absurd about it. A species intelligent enough to sequence genomes and build particle accelerators, trapped in outcomes that a straightforward vote would overturn. The problem isn't that people are bad or stupid. It's that individual incentives and collective outcomes come apart, and we don't have good machinery for pulling them back together. Every soldier in a trench would rather be home. Every farmer using the harmful practice would rather everyone stopped. But unilateral defection just means you lose.

So I'd want whatever it is — better institutions, better ability to make and trust binding commitments, some capacity for reliable common knowledge of what everyone actually prefers — that lets people escape those traps.

I'll admit some uncertainty about whether this is the right pick. A case could be made that I should just say "end the suffering of the billions of animals in factory farms" or "cure aging," something with a clearer, larger number attached. And I notice I might be drawn to the coordination answer partly because it's intellectually elegant, which is a bias worth flagging rather than hiding.

But I keep coming back to it because it's upstream of so much else. If you fix a specific catastrophe, you fix that catastrophe. If you fix the thing that generates catastrophes nobody wanted, you get the others as they come — including ones we haven't invented yet. And there will be new ones. That seems worth more than any single repair.

The honest caveat: I don't know if that's a change you *could* make, versus a permanent feature of what it means for many minds to share a world.
